chunks: Ali ibn al-Nu'man narrated from Ibn Muskān, from Dāwūd ibn Abī Yazīd, from Abū Shaybah al-Zuhrī, from Abū Jaʿfar (peace be upon him) who said:

The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Death! Death! Death comes with whatever is in it; it brings comfort and ease, and a blessed return to the lofty heavens for the people of the eternal abode – those who had struggled for it and yearned for it. And death comes with whatever is in it; it brings wretchedness and regret, and a return of [great] loss to a scorching fire for the people of the abode of delusion – those who strived for it and yearned for it.'
And he (peace be upon him) said: 'When the guardianship of Satan and wretchedness is deserved, aspiration comes in front of the eyes and [remembrance of] death goes behind the back.'

He [also] said: 'The Messenger of Allah (peace be upon him and his family) was asked, “Who among the believers are cleverer?” He said, “Those among them who remember death more often and make more intense preparations for it.”'
ai.seo_question: What is the significance of remembering death in Shia Islamic teachings?
ai.summary: In *Kitab al-Zuhd*, this hadith from Imam al-Sadiq (AS) underscores the Shia concept of *al-dhikr al-mawt* (remembrance of death) as the hallmark of the 'keenest' (*aknas*) believer, linking spiritual preparedness directly to the quality of one's transition. It contrasts the 'blessed ball' of the righteous with the 'losing ball' of the deluded, illustrating how false hope (*al-amal*) obscures the reality of death for those under Satan's influence. This narrative reinforces the ascetic tradition's focus on aligning one's deeds with the ultimate destination, whether eternal bliss or regretful punishment.
